mmat_comments: The study compares results from a survey of healthcare professionals 1 month before the intervention (September 2014) with a survey one year later (September 2015). There were no significant differences comparing 2014 and 2015, but the results also show that "66% of physicians who interacted with the clinical components of the initiative demonstrated significant attitude changes". It is unclear how this change is measured - is it from the follow-up survey only, comparing participants who did vs. did not interact with the programme?

Brief description of study findings: There was no evidence that participants in 2015 and different attitudes or knowledge than those in 2014. However, the key results (comparing results from 2014 with 2015) do not seem to support the conclusion that the programme "significantly improved general internists’ attitudes, preparedness, and clinical practice".

intervention_description: Low-threshold ED buprenorphine treatment at 52 hospitals participating in the CA Bridge Program. The bridge programme included active patient navigation to outpatient addiction treatment; and harm reduction (overdose education and naloxone). Brief description of study findings: 7000/12,000 patients with OUD received buprenorphine, which was interpreted as an increase. Hospitals continued providing buprenorphine after support via the VA Bridge programme ended. Authors also concluded that "the multicomponent CA Bridge model, including low threshold ED buprenorphine, connection to outpatient addiction treatment, and promotion of a harm reduction approach, resulted in sustainable institutional change". Substance use navigators were considered key to the success of the model, particularly due to their training in motivational interviewing and expert knowledge.

Brief description of study findings:
Compared with an inpatient detoxification protocol, initiation of and linkage to buprenorphine treatment is an effective means for engaging medically hospitalized patients who are not seeking addiction treatment and reduces illicit opioid use 6 months after hospitalization. However, maintaining engagement in treatment remains a challenge. Brief description of study outcomes-  quantifying outcomes:
1. Follow up:  Participants randomized to the linkage group had higher observed follow-up rates at all periods. Betweengroup differences in follow-up rates were not statistically significant at 1 or 3 months. The linkage group had a significantly higher rate of follow-up at 6 months (?2 = 6.75, P = .009).
2. Opiate use during follow up period - Relative to those randomized to the detoxification group, the estimated odds of reporting any illicit opioid use were significantly lower among those randomized to the linkage group (OR, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.04-0.77; P = .003). On the basis of complete case analysis, the estimated rate of illicit opioid use in those in the linkage group was approximately 40% lower
(IRR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.46-0.73;P < .01) than for participants randomized to the detoxification group. The predicted rates of use were 8.6 (linkage group) vs 13.7 (detoxification group) days of illicit opioid use per 30 follow-up days.

Brief description of study findings:
Emergency departments can be an appropriate setting for initiating opioid agonist treatment, but to be sustained, it likely needs to be coupled with community-based follow-up and support to ensure longer-term retention. intervention_description: A multidisciplinary team to care for patients with drug use associated infective endocarditis (DUA-IE), termed the DUET team,  was created in August 2018. The team consists of a core group of members, including cardiac surgeons, infectious disease specialists, addiction medicine specialists, and cardiologists. The goal of the DUET team is to provide a regular forum for multiple specialties to discuss their shared patients with DUA-IE. Primary team members, interventional cardiologists, neurologists, neurosurgeons, nurses, pharmacists, substance use disorder recovery coaches, case managers, and social workers are also routinely invited. To facilitate reporting of patients with DUA-IE by frontline providers to the DUET team, a web-based survey via the REDCap electronic data capture tool was developed. Providers are asked to provide basic patient data and specify whether an expedited meeting is needed because of complex or time-sensitive case elements. Engagement of the DUET team is standard practice when the CT surgery service is consulted by the primary team for a patient who injects drugs.

intervention_description: The inpatient opioid withdrawal guidelines were developed by an interdisciplinary task force including pharmacists, physicians, nurses, psychologists, social workers, security personnel, and hospital administrators.
